_comment: The CSRF contract: ONE answer key, four frameworks. Feature 37.
CSRF protection uses a signed formToken (a JWT) delivered in the form body or
the X-Form-Token header and validated on state-changing writes by CsrfMiddleware.
This fixture pins the behaviour every framework must share after the CSRF-DEC-01
(secret fail-closed) and CSRF-DEC-02 (env auto-wire + session-bind + type=form)
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework and a list of case names.
The four suites carry the SAME case names in each language's own idiom (Python
snake_case method, PHP testPascalCase method, Ruby it-description, Node assert
label), which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py normalises and matches. Python
is the REFERENCE implementation; the shapes asserted here are the canonical ones
the other three move to. Real HS256, real Request pipeline, real Frond token

invariants.rule: With TINA4_SECRET unset the CSRF middleware fails CLOSED: a formToken forged with the retired public 'tina4-default-secret', AND one forged with the blank '' key, are both REJECTED 403. There is no shipped named default, and a blank HMAC key is publicly reproducible, so no token can be trusted when the secret is blank.
invariants.why: The formToken doubles as a write-route auth credential, so a forgeable token is a CSRF bypass AND an auth bypass. PHP shipped a live 'tina4-default-secret' fallback (plus an $_ENV mutation that poisoned the whole process JWT secret); Node's generator signed with 'tina4-default-secret' while its validator used '' - legit tokens rejected AND ''-forged tokens accepted. Both are closed here.
cases: forged default secret token is rejected
forged blank secret token is rejected

invariants.rule: A formToken produced by the REAL Frond generator ({{ form_token() }}) with TINA4_SECRET set validates and passes the middleware. Generator and validator resolve the SAME fail-closed secret, so a legitimately-rendered token is never self-rejected.
invariants.why: Node's generator/validator secret split rejected legitimately-rendered tokens (a self-inflicted 403 for real users), and PHP's generator signed with the wrong value entirely. The positive case proves the generator and validator agree.
cases: a frond emitted form token passes csrf

invariants.rule: The token's type claim MUST be "form". A validly-signed but non-form JWT (e.g. an auth/session token) presented in the formToken slot is REJECTED 403 even though its signature verifies.
invariants.why: Without the type check any valid JWT was accepted in the formToken slot, widening the credential that satisfies a write. Enforcing type==form scopes the formToken to its purpose.
cases: a non form jwt in the form token slot is rejected

invariants.rule: When the token carries a session_id and the request session's id differs, the write is REJECTED 403. A token minted for one session cannot be replayed against another.
invariants.why: A signed nonce with no session binding rests entirely on secret secrecy; binding the token to the session defeats cross-session replay.
cases: a token bound to a foreign session is rejected

invariants.rule: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe methods and skip CSRF validation entirely - a GET with no token passes.
invariants.why: CSRF gates state change; safe methods do not change state and must never be blocked for lacking a token.
cases: a safe get request skips csrf

invariants.rule: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE are gated: a write with no formToken is REJECTED 403.
invariants.why: State-changing methods are exactly what CSRF must protect; a missing token is a failed check, not a pass.
cases: a post without a token is rejected

invariants.rule: A write route marked @noauth / ->noAuth() / .noAuth / secure:false skips CSRF - a genuinely public endpoint (login, webhook) has no session to protect.
invariants.why: CSRF binds to a session; a public endpoint has none, so the token requirement would only break legitimate public POSTs.
cases: a noauth write route skips csrf

invariants.rule: A request with a valid Authorization: Bearer JWT skips CSRF - an API client authenticating per-request is not subject to the cookie-replay attack CSRF defends against.
invariants.why: CSRF is a browser/cookie attack; a Bearer-authenticated API client supplies its own credential each call and cannot be CSRF'd.
cases: a valid bearer token skips csrf

invariants.rule: A formToken presented in the URL query string is REJECTED 403 - a token in the URL leaks through logs, referers and history.
invariants.why: A URL query is logged and shared; accepting a token there would leak the credential. The token must ride the body or the X-Form-Token header only.
cases: a form token in the query string is rejected

invariants.rule: CSRF is OFF by default (the middleware is NOT attached, so a default app has no CSRF gate); setting TINA4_CSRF=true (or 1/yes/on) ATTACHES CsrfMiddleware at boot so every write is gated. The env flag is the switch - it is no longer inert.
invariants.why: Before this the flag was read only AFTER a manual attach, so TINA4_CSRF=true alone did nothing and the docstrings claimed protection a default app did not have. Now the flag genuinely controls attachment.

invariants.rule: Every CSRF rejection is an HTTP 403 whose JSON body carries the CSRF_INVALID code. The rejection envelope is identical across the four frameworks.
invariants.why: A real client must be able to recognise a CSRF failure by one stable code and status regardless of the framework serving it.
cases: the rejection body is the csrf invalid envelope
